notes.meaning: Paul explained why the leaders in Jerusalem rejected Jesus. Even though they heard the writings of the prophets read aloud every Sabbath, they did not recognize who Jesus was. Without knowing it, by condemning Him to death they actually fulfilled the very prophecies they read each week.

The rulers found no legal crime or wrongdoing in Jesus that called for a death penalty. Even so, they insisted that the Roman governor Pilate order Him to be killed. His death was an unjust act of human hatred, but it was still part of God's plan.

When the rulers finished doing everything the scriptures foretold about His suffering, Jesus was taken down from the cross and laid in a stone tomb. Calling the cross a tree reminds readers of the ancient law that anyone hanged on wood was under a curse, which Jesus took on Himself. Friendly Jewish leaders then gave His body a proper burial.

Human judges put Jesus to death, but God completely overturned their verdict. God brought Him back from the dead by His mighty power. This resurrection was the clearest proof possible that Jesus is innocent and truly God's Messiah.

Jesus did not disappear after rising from the dead, but showed Himself alive over forty days. The disciples who had traveled with Him from Galilee down to Jerusalem saw Him again and again. Those eyewitnesses were chosen to testify about His resurrection to the Jewish people.

Paul and Barnabas brought joyful news that God had fulfilled the ancient promise made to Abraham and David. God completed that promise for their children by raising Jesus from the dead. Quoting the second Psalm, Paul explained that the resurrection publicly showed Jesus to be God's true Son and King.

God raised Jesus to live forever, never to die or rot away in the grave like others who were brought back to life only to die again. Paul supported this from Isaiah, where God promised David reliable and holy blessings. For those royal promises to never fail, the King who rules must never die again.

Paul cited another passage from Psalm 16, where David said God would not let His Holy One see decay. This prophecy pointed forward to someone whose body would never decompose in the tomb. It promised a complete triumph over the grave.

King David faithfully served God's plan during his own lifetime, but then he died and was buried beside his ancestors. His human body decayed in the earth just like any other person. This proves that David could not have been writing about himself in that Psalm.

Jesus is the only One whose body never rotted, because God raised Him on the third day. Since David decayed and Jesus did not, the ancient prophecy pointed solely to Jesus. He alone is the living Savior who conquered the power of death.

Paul arrived at the heart of his message by announcing forgiveness of sins through Jesus. Forgiveness means God cancels the debt of our sins so they are never held against us. This clean slate is freely offered to everyone who hears the gospel.

Through Jesus, everyone who believes is justified, which means declared righteous and innocent before God. The law of Moses commanded sacrifices, but those rituals could never remove human guilt or change the heart. Trusting in Christ accomplishes what the law could never do.

Paul gave a solemn warning from the prophet Habakkuk so his hearers would not reject God's message. In ancient times, God sent foreign armies in judgment, and people refused to believe it would happen until it was too late. Scoffing at God's offer of salvation brings a far worse and eternal ruin.

As Paul and Barnabas were leaving the synagogue, people in the audience begged them to speak about these truths again on the following Sabbath. The message had made a deep impression, and they wanted more time to think and ask questions. Many were eager to hear the good news a second time.

When the meeting broke up, many Jews and Gentile converts to Judaism followed the apostles. Paul and Barnabas talked with them and urged them to keep living in God's grace, which is His free and undeserved favor. Real faith means continuing to trust God even when troubles arise.

By the next Sabbath, excitement about the apostles' message had spread so widely that nearly the whole city gathered to listen. Gentiles joined the usual worshipers, creating a crowd far too large for an ordinary room. People came with an intense desire to hear what God had to say.

When certain Jewish leaders saw the huge crowds, they were filled with bitter jealousy. They did not want Gentiles to be treated as equal members in God's kingdom without adopting Jewish laws. To tear down the apostles, they began shouting objections and insulting the name of Jesus.

Paul and Barnabas spoke with great courage, saying it was God's plan to bring the message to the Jewish people first. But since those leaders rejected it, they showed by their own choice that they were refusing eternal life. Because of their hard hearts, the apostles turned to share the gospel directly with the Gentiles.

The apostles showed from Scripture that God had commanded them to reach other nations. In the book of Isaiah, God declared that His servant would be a light to the Gentiles and bring salvation across the whole earth. Paul and Barnabas saw this prophecy as their direct calling from the Lord.

The Gentiles were overjoyed to hear that God's door was open to them, and they praised the Lord's word. All who were appointed for eternal life put their trust in Jesus. God welcomed these new believers without requiring them to become Jewish first.

differ.view: God chose specific individuals before time to receive eternal life, and this appointment is the reason they believed.
The verse describes people who were ready and disposed in their hearts to accept eternal life when they heard the gospel, not an eternal decree.

notes.meaning: The message about the Lord quickly spread through the whole surrounding area. New converts carried the good news back to their homes, farms, and neighboring villages. God's truth gained ground and changed lives throughout the entire district.

Opponents stirred up wealthy Gentile women who attended the synagogue, along with the leading men of the city. They used this political influence to start persecution against Paul and Barnabas and force them out of town. Worldly power was used to try to halt the spread of the gospel.

Before leaving, Paul and Barnabas shook the dust off their feet as a warning, just as Jesus had taught His followers to do. This public sign showed they had done their duty, leaving those who rejected the message responsible for their own choice. Then the two missionaries traveled on to continue their work in Iconium.

Even though their teachers were forced out, the new believers in Antioch were filled with great joy and the Holy Spirit. God gave them inner peace and confidence that did not depend on an easy life. The trouble around them could not extinguish the joy Christ had given them.
